meta.tier_interpretation_note: Tier thresholds (8×, 2–8×, >1×, else) are treated as biological outcomes. Likelihood scores reflect how likely each legal standard is to be a meaningful driver of achieving that tier outcome assuming active enforcement/implementation; this is a plausibility mapping, not a guarantee.

Legal Standards.name: Federal Endangered Species Act (ESA) (16 U.S.C. §1531 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: For listed salmonids (and listed species that share the system), ESA drives project operations (CVP/SWP), flow/temperature constraints, fish passage/entrainment requirements, and habitat protection through consultation and enforceable measures.

key_elements.plain_definition: When a federal agency must check that its actions won’t push a listed species toward extinction or wreck its critical habitat.
The expert agency’s document that says whether the action causes “jeopardy” and, if so, lists required fixes (including BiOps for CVP/SWP long-term operations).
Required operational/habitat changes that allow a project to proceed without “jeopardy.”
Harm/kill that happens as a side effect of otherwise lawful action, regulated under ESA.

Legal Standards.name: California Endangered Species Act (CESA) (Fish & Game Code §2050 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: State analogue to ESA for California-listed species; commonly affects state and local projects and can constrain water infrastructure/operations when “take” of listed species is possible.

key_elements.plain_definition: A permit CDFW can issue allowing incidental take if impacts are minimized/avoided and fully mitigated.

Legal Standards.name: Federal Clean Water Act (CWA) — especially §401 + water quality standards (33 U.S.C. §1251 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: Salmon depend on cold, clean water and functioning river/estuary habitat. CWA influences dredge/fill permits, hydropower licensing, diversions, and restoration projects through enforceable water quality conditions.

key_elements.plain_definition: Before a federal permit/license can be issued, the state must certify the project will comply with water quality standards (and can attach conditions or deny). California Water Boards administer this.

Legal Standards.name: Porter-Cologne Water Quality Control Act (California Water Code §13000 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: Backbone of California water quality law; requires Water Boards to set beneficial uses and water quality objectives (including fish habitat uses) via Basin Plans.

key_elements.plain_definition: What a waterbody is used for (including ecosystem uses like fish habitat).
Numeric/narrative thresholds meant to protect those uses.

Legal Standards.name: SWRCB Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan (Bay-Delta Plan) (under CWA + Porter-Cologne)
Legal Standards.note: Sets water quality/flow-related objectives for the Bay-Delta system (including protections “for fish and wildlife”), influencing Delta outflow, salinity, flow regimes, and related operations that affect salmon migration and survival.

Legal Standards.name: Central Valley Project Improvement Act (CVPIA) (1992) (Pub. L. 102-575, Title XXXIV)
Legal Standards.note: Requires operational and restoration improvements for fish and wildlife connected to the CVP; tied to the salmon “doubling goal” concept in Central Valley restoration work.

Legal Standards.name: California Fish & Game Code §5937 (dam flow requirement)
Legal Standards.note: Requires dam owners to pass “sufficient water” to keep fish downstream “in good condition,” which can translate into minimum flow releases relevant to salmonids below dams.

key_elements.plain_definition: Passage structure for fish to move around a dam/barrier.

Legal Standards.name: Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (MSA) — Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) provisions (16 U.S.C. §1801 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: Requires federal agencies to consult on actions that may adversely affect essential fish habitat; NOAA Fisheries uses this to recommend conservation measures that can matter for salmon (including in California water-operations contexts).

Legal Standards.name: California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) (Pub. Res. Code §21000 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: Forces disclosure/analysis and feasible mitigation/alternatives for significant environmental impacts of discretionary projects, often shaping project design for instream habitat, temperature, passage, and construction impacts.

Legal Standards.name: Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta Reform Act of 2009 (Water Code §85000 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: Establishes the Delta Stewardship Council and “coequal goals” including protecting/restoring the Delta ecosystem; can constrain/shape state actions and consistency findings under the Delta Plan.

Tier 1.threshold: ≥ 80% chance that salmon population grows 8× its starting size, using a rolling 10-year average

policies.note: Can force major operational constraints and habitat protections, but 8× over a 10-year rolling average usually requires broad, sustained system improvements beyond ESA alone.
Strong on specific projects, but not typically a system-wide growth-multiplier instrument.

policies.policy_name: Clean Water Act (CWA) §401 + water quality standards
policies.note: Water quality tools alone rarely generate basin-wide 8× growth.
Foundational but often indirect; depends on how aggressively objectives and enforcement are set.

policies.policy_name: Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan (Bay-Delta Plan)
policies.note: Even strong flow objectives are rarely sufficient by themselves to yield 8× results across runs/regions.
Fish-forward and tied to “doubling goal” concepts, but still doesn’t guarantee very high multipliers given ocean/drought/habitat constraints.
Applies dam-by-dam; powerful locally but not always system-wide and doesn’t automatically solve passage, habitat, Delta survival, etc.
EFH consultation yields conservation recommendations, but often has weaker enforcement teeth than ESA/CWA.
Procedural statute; can shape projects but does not mandate biological outcomes.

policies.policy_name: Delta Reform Act / Delta Plan consistency
policies.note: Governance framework; indirect lever for outcomes.

Tier 2.threshold: ≥ 80% chance that salmon population grows 2×–8× its starting size, using a rolling 10-year average

policies.note: Plausible where ESA-driven operations and habitat actions reduce mortality/entrainment and improve flows/temperatures.
Can meaningfully shape state-led projects/operations, especially when paired with water board requirements and habitat restoration.

policies.policy_name: Clean Water Act (CWA) §401 + water quality standards
policies.note: Strong when §401 conditions materially improve temperature, sediment, toxics, and habitat impacts of licensed/permitted actions.
Can drive meaningful improvements through basin planning and enforcement where fish habitat objectives are stringent.

policies.policy_name: Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan (Bay-Delta Plan)
policies.note: Flow + salinity regimes can be a big lever depending on final objectives and compliance.

policies.relationship: Most to moderately likely driver of Tier 2
policies.note: Among the stronger legal hooks because it explicitly targets fish/wildlife outcomes tied to CVP management.
Can materially improve below-dam instream conditions where flow is the binding constraint.

policies.relationship: Least to moderately likely driver of Tier 2
policies.note: Can help if recommendations are adopted and meaningfully address habitat bottlenecks.

policies.relationship: Least to moderately likely driver of Tier 2
policies.note: Can matter a lot for specific projects, but not a guaranteed driver of basin-wide multipliers.

policies.policy_name: Delta Reform Act / Delta Plan consistency
policies.relationship: Least to moderately likely driver of Tier 2
policies.note: Can constrain projects to better align with ecosystem protection/restoration as part of “coequal goals.”

Tier 3.threshold: ≥ 80% chance that salmon population exceeds its starting size, using a rolling 10-year average

policies.note: Preventing “jeopardy” and protecting critical habitat tends to push management toward at least avoiding net decline.
Frequent use case is preventing/mitigating take to avoid worsening conditions.

policies.policy_name: Clean Water Act (CWA) §401 + water quality standards
policies.note: Very commonly relevant to preventing degradation of core habitat/water quality prerequisites.
Often the legal backbone for maintaining baseline water quality needed to avoid decline.

policies.policy_name: Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan (Bay-Delta Plan)
policies.note: One of the most direct state instruments for fish/wildlife-protective flow and water-quality constraints in the system.
Very likely relevant to sustaining improvement above baseline when implemented robustly.

policies.relationship: Most to moderately likely driver of Tier 3
policies.note: Likely to help achieve “>1×” in reaches where low flow/temperature stress is the major driver.
Moderate likelihood of supporting incremental improvement/protection, especially for habitat-related actions.
Often helps prevent avoidable harm and requires feasible mitigation.

policies.policy_name: Delta Reform Act / Delta Plan consistency
policies.note: Helps maintain ecosystem restoration as a legally embedded objective in Delta decision-making.

Tier 4.threshold: Assigned if Tier 1, Tier 2, or Tier 3 is not satisfied (i.e., no outcome guarantee of >1× growth at ≥80% probability)

policies.relationship: Tier 4 indicates protections/constraints may be binding (context-dependent)
policies.note: If salmon trends are flat/declining, ESA constraints often become central in shaping operations and habitat measures (where listings/critical habitat apply).

policies.relationship: Tier 4 indicates protections/constraints may be binding (context-dependent)
policies.note: When listed species are at risk, take-avoidance and mitigation requirements become more salient for state and local actions.

policies.policy_name: Clean Water Act (CWA) §401 + water quality standards
policies.relationship: Tier 4 indicates prevention of further degradation becomes critical
policies.note: In poor conditions, enforceable water quality conditions (temperature/toxics/sediment/habitat) are key to stabilizing habitat prerequisites.

policies.relationship: Tier 4 indicates baseline protections and enforcement are central
policies.note: Water-quality objectives and beneficial use protections are central to avoiding continued decline.

policies.policy_name: Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan (Bay-Delta Plan)
policies.relationship: Tier 4 indicates flow/water-quality constraints may be especially consequential
policies.note: If Tier 4 reflects poor survival/migration conditions, flow/salinity/outflow constraints become especially consequential where applicable.

policies.relationship: Tier 4 suggests restoration/ops improvements are needed but not sufficient alone
policies.note: Fish-forward restoration and operational improvements are relevant, but outcomes depend on multiple system and ocean drivers.

policies.relationship: Tier 4 can indicate local below-dam flow conditions are limiting (reach-specific)
policies.note: Where low below-dam releases are a limiting factor, §5937-related flow requirements can be pivotal on a project-by-project basis.

policies.relationship: Tier 4 suggests stronger habitat recommendations may be relevant but adoption varies
policies.note: EFH consultations may intensify focus on habitat impacts, but recommendations may have weaker enforcement than ESA/CWA.

policies.relationship: Tier 4 increases salience of mitigation/alternatives for harmful projects (project-specific)
policies.note: Doesn’t mandate recovery, but can require mitigation and alternatives to reduce further harm from discretionary projects.

policies.policy_name: Delta Reform Act / Delta Plan consistency
policies.relationship: Tier 4 heightens governance emphasis on ecosystem restoration (indirect)
policies.note: Supports keeping ecosystem restoration legally embedded in Delta decision-making, but acts indirectly through consistency/oversight.

Governing Agencies.name: NOAA Fisheries (NMFS)
Governing Agencies.note: Implements ESA for anadromous salmonids via Section 7 consultations/BiOps and oversees EFH consultations and conservation recommendations under Magnuson-Stevens.

Governing Agencies.name: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (USFWS)
Governing Agencies.note: Supports CVPIA fish program coordination/data and the ‘doubling goal’ concept; also implements ESA for species under its jurisdiction.

Governing Agencies.name: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (USBR)
Governing Agencies.note: Operates the Central Valley Project; operating plans trigger ESA Section 7 consultation and NEPA analysis; implements CVPIA-related actions through CVP operations.

Governing Agencies.name: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE)
Governing Agencies.note: Issues federal permits that can trigger CWA §404/§401 processes and ESA consultation when aquatic habitat is affected (project-specific triggers vary).

Governing Agencies.name: State Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB) + Regional Water Quality Control Boards
Governing Agencies.note: Implement Porter-Cologne; set Basin Plans and objectives; administer CWA §401 certifications; develop/implement the Bay-Delta Plan.

Governing Agencies.name: California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW)
Governing Agencies.note: Implements CESA (including ITPs); serves as CEQA trustee/responsible agency providing biological review for projects.

Governing Agencies.name: California Department of Water Resources (DWR)
Governing Agencies.note: Operates the State Water Project; actions can trigger CESA processes and interact with ESA constraints through coordinated operations with CVP/SWP; operates in a Bay-Delta Plan compliance context.

Governing Agencies.name: Delta Stewardship Council (DSC)
Governing Agencies.note: Created by the Delta Reform Act; adopts and oversees the Delta Plan and consistency framework to further the ‘coequal goals.’

Governing Agencies.name: California Fish and Game Commission
Governing Agencies.note: Lists species under CESA (regulatory trigger for protections).

Governing Agencies.name: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC)
Governing Agencies.note: Hydropower licensing can trigger CWA §401 certification conditions from California Water Boards and often intersects with ESA consultations for project effects on listed species.
